blocks.md:
Saving keeps money safe. Investing helps money **grow**.

When you invest, you buy something you hope will be worth more later. Over long periods, investing has usually grown faster than savings accounts. But it also comes with risk. Values go up and down.

**Before you invest**
• Build an emergency fund first
• Only invest money you won't need for at least 5 years
• Pay off high-interest debt, like credit cards

**Why start young?**
Time lets compound growth do its work. Small amounts invested early can grow more than bigger amounts invested later.
**Parent tip:** Kids can't open a brokerage account alone. A parent can open a custodial account for them. If your teen has earned income, a custodial Roth IRA is another option.

**Stocks**
A stock is a small piece of a company. If the company does well, your piece may be worth more. Some companies also pay **dividends**, a share of profits.

Stocks can swing a lot, especially over short periods.

**Bonds**
A bond is a loan you make to a company or a government. They pay you interest and give your money back on a set date.

Bonds are usually steadier than stocks, but they tend to grow more slowly.

**The basic trade-off**
• Stocks: more growth, more ups and downs
• Bonds: less growth, more stability

Most investors use a mix of both.

options: Lending money that's paid back with interest
question.explanation: When you buy a bond you lend money to a company or government. They pay interest and return the money later.

blocks.md:
Picking single stocks is hard, even for experts. Funds make it easier.

**Mutual funds**
A fund pools money from many people to buy lots of investments at once.

**Index funds**
These copy a list of companies, like the S&P 500. They don't try to pick winners. They just own the whole list.

**ETFs**
Exchange-traded funds also hold many investments. They trade during the day like a single stock. Many ETFs are index funds.

**Why people like index funds**
• Instant diversification
• Usually low fees
• Simple to understand

**Watch the fees**
A fund's yearly fee is its **expense ratio**. A difference of 1% a year can cost a lot over decades. Lower is better.

blocks.md:
A portfolio is everything you invest in. Simple is usually best.

**Match it to your timeline**
• Money needed in under 5 years: keep it mostly safe, like savings or short-term bonds
• Money for 10+ years: you can usually take more stock risk

**A simple starter idea**
Many beginners use one broad index fund, or a mix of a stock index fund and a bond index fund.

**Target-date funds**
These pick a mix based on when you'll need the money. They get safer as that date gets closer.

**Keep it balanced**
Once a year, check your mix. If stocks grew a lot, move some back to bonds. This is called rebalancing.

**Invest a little, often**
Putting in the same amount regularly is called dollar-cost averaging. You buy more when prices are low and less when they're high.

**Don't panic**
Markets drop sometimes. Selling in a panic can lock in losses. Long-term investors usually ride it out.

**Skip the hype**
If friends or social media say a stock is a "sure thing," be careful. Nobody can promise that.

**Keep costs low**
High fees quietly eat your returns.

**Keep learning**
Read, ask questions and start small.
**Scam alert:** "Guaranteed" high returns are a red flag. Real investments always carry risk.

options: To pick the single best stock
To spread risk across many investments
question.hint: Don't put all your eggs in one basket.
question.explanation: Owning many investments means one bad one hurts less. It lowers risk but can't remove it.
